title: Stellar Red Giant Above KPNO
caption: Betelgeuse above the Bok 2.3-meter Telescope, Kitt Peak National Observatory
celestial: Landscape photograph; the source does not name the site

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A single orange star stands out at the center of a multicolored night sky above the UArizona Bok 2.3-meter Telescope at NSF NOIRLab's Kitt Peak National Observatory (KPNO). Faraway city lights, passing cars, airglow and the Milky Way's arc all add to the mix of colors. On the right, zodiacal light rising from the horizon crosses the Milky Way.

The orange star is Betelgeuse, a red supergiant that marks a shoulder of Orion, the hunter. As a relatively old star it glows a cooler red than its hot blue neighbors, but it is usually still the 10th brightest star in the night sky. It is also enormous, more than 750 times the Sun's diameter, so no bigger star can be seen without a telescope.

In 2019 astronomers saw a small explosion on its surface, and the news fed speculation that a supernova was near. In 2021 scientists concluded that the dying star will not explode for at least another 100,000 years.

understand.summary: A night-sky landscape photograph by T. Slovinský. No camera or exposure details or color mapping are published.
understand.eye: A long camera exposure gathers more light than the eye, so the night sky would look fainter to someone standing at the site.

explore: The photograph was taken by T. Slovinský during the NOIRLab 2022 Photo Expedition, which visited all of NOIRLab's sites. NOIRLab released it as one of its Image of the Week features.
alt: An orange star at the center of a multicolored night sky above the Bok telescope at Kitt Peak, with the arc of the Milky Way.
